title: Why one big convoy beat four small ones
description:
Put 100 ships in four square convoys of 25 and the escorts have 80 ship-widths of edge to guard; one square of 100 has only 40, so the same escorts stand twice as close. A U-boat finds a big convoy about as easily as a small one, and once inside it sinks a few ships either way, so the share you lose falls as the convoy grows. Patrick Blackett's operational research team showed it from two years of records: convoys averaging 32 ships lost 2.5%, convoys averaging 54 lost 1.1%. In spring 1943 the Admiralty dropped its 60-ship limit and convoys of up to 100 ships crossed the Atlantic.

Numbers checked in code (edge lengths of square convoys, and 100,000 simulated U-boat attacks on an evenly spaced escort line). Sources: warhistory.org/2020/09/06/may-1943-climax-in-the-atlantic-i/ and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operations_research

beats.say: Your ships are safer in one big convoy than in four small ones.
Not because it hides better. A U-boat finds a big convoy about as easily as a small one. So four convoys are four targets.
The Atlantic, 1942. The navy's rule: 40 ships is best, 60 is the limit.
Pack your 100 ships into squares. Four squares of 25 have an edge 80 ships long. One square of 100: just 40.
Your escorts guard the edge. Same escorts, half the edge: they stand twice as close, and U-boats get in where the line is thin.
But what about the U-boat that does get in?
It sinks a few ships either way. In a big convoy, that's a few out of 100, not out of 25.
Patrick Blackett checked the records. Convoys of about 32 ships lost 2.5%. Convoys of 54 lost just 1.1%. By 1943, convoys of 100 were crossing.
So with 400 ships in one square, how much more edge than 100?
